blurb: Fanout's 301-lesson machine learning mathematics course, mapped through its free course pages, six free sample lessons on sets, and its Math Decoder notation tool.

adaptedFrom.name: Fanout (Suraj Gaud)
adaptedFrom.note: Fanout publishes no open licence on its site; Sikhi University has Fanout's written permission to build this reading map. No lesson text or worked example is reproduced here — every card opens the real page at fanout.sh. Six of the course's 301 lessons are free samples; the remainder sit behind Fanout's paid Pro plans.

modules.title: The course map
modules.objective: See the shape of Fanout's twelve-module mathematics path — sets, linear algebra, calculus, probability, and inference — before starting the free sample lessons.
modules.teach: The math course underpins both the AI research and ML math phases the AI School already teaches — think of it as a second, more exhaustive pass, structured as 301 short topic-level lessons rather than long chapters. This module is free; the lessons it maps are mostly paid.

modules.title: Six free sample lessons on sets
modules.objective: Work through Fanout's free set-theory lessons — set-builder notation, indicator functions, Cartesian products, argmax and argmin, suprema, and interior/boundary points — as a sample of the course's teaching style.
modules.teach: These are Fanout's own selected free lessons out of 301. Set theory is the course's first module, so this is also a fair test of whether the ground-up, topic-by-topic pace suits you before any paid commitment.

labs.title: Describe planar regions in set-builder notation
How to find argmax and argmin in tables and graphs
When is a supremum not a maximum
How to identify interior and boundary points in R²

modules.title: The Math Decoder
modules.objective: Use Fanout's Math Decoder to look up unfamiliar notation the moment it stalls a paper, by glyph, pronunciation, LaTeX, or meaning.
modules.teach: This is the tool worth bookmarking independently of the course: paste in the symbol you don't recognise from a paper and get a plain-English decoding, cross-referenced to a worked formula where one exists. It's free and permanently public.

labs.title: Math Decoder for AI Research Papers
